finding.summary: Tenant identity comes from a header the client controls (X-Tenant), so an authenticated user can read or change another tenant's data.

claims.text: The PRD says the API reads the tenant from the X-Tenant request header on every request. Nothing ties that value to the authenticated user's session. Any logged-in user can set X-Tenant to another tenant's ID and get that tenant's data (cross-tenant IDOR / broken access control).

Authentication is only email and password (line 2), and sessions never expire (line 4). Nothing in the PRD binds a session to a tenant, so one stolen or long-lived session could be pointed at any tenant indefinitely, which makes the impact worse.

recommendations: Work out the tenant on the server from the authenticated session or token claims. Do not trust X-Tenant. If the header stays (for example, for users who belong to several tenants), check it against the user's tenant memberships on every request and reject any mismatch.
Add an authorization check at the data-access layer that scopes every query to the tenant bound to the session.
Separately, set an expiry and idle timeout for sessions (line 4).
questions: Can a user belong to more than one tenant? If so, how is the active tenant chosen and checked?
